title: Tories dismiss PM’s budget ‘everyday fixes’ as little more than ‘cheaper gherkins’, and ‘an insult to families’ – UK politics live

blocks.text: Unison says focus on cost of living, including tax-free mileage, 'commendable', but 'bolder' policies needed

Unison has particularly welcomed the announcement today about higher tax-free mileage rates being made permanent. (See 9.07am.) The union has been campaigning for this, and some of its members will benefit.
But, in her response, Andrea Egan, Unison’s general secretary illustrated how there is a limit to how much goodwill a government can generate from small “everyday fixes”. She said:

double quotation markThese are welcome measures, especially making the uplift to mileage rates permanent, something Unison has campaigned hard for. The government’s relentless focus on the cost of living is commendable. But the cost of essentials, including food and fuel, is going to keep soaring, meaning breathing space will quickly be closed down. That’s why we need to see a bolder approach, based on making the wealthy pay their fair share and improving the lives of working-class communities in a more enduring way.
The Treasury says three million people are expected to benefit from the mileage changes. It says:

double quotation markThese changes will provide £120 a year in additional tax savings for a worker doing 6,000 business miles, with someone driving 15,000 business miles receiving up to £300 in additional tax savings.
Tories dismiss PM’s budget ‘everyday fixes’ as little more than ‘cheaper gherkins’, and ‘an insult to families

Good morning. Prime ministers tend to get judged by posterity by the decisions they take on the big issues of the day. But little things matter too in the here and now, often disproportionately, and Andy Burnham, more than his predecessors, has decided that what he calls “everyday fixes” are worth focusing on too. Alexandra Topping wrote a good analysis about the pluses and minuses of this approach last week. But she filed too soon, because this morning Burnham has announced another five.

These are all changes contained in tomorrow’s budget but being announced today – presumably because John Healey will have bigger surprises for MPs tomorrow, and the Treasury wants these measures to get some media attention today because tomorrow they will be overshadowed by another story.

One of the measures is of particular interest to the Guardian because we have highlighted the scandal that led to hundreds of thousands of people getting the carer’s allowance being ordered to pay back huge sums of money because inadvertently their weekly earnings went slightly above the threshold allowed. In other parts of the welfare system, people just have to return the overpayment, but the rules for carer’s allowance were draconian, and a tiny breach of the weekly earnings allowance could lead to people being ordered to pay back thousands of pounds.
As Patrick Butler and Pippa Crerar report in our splash, this rule is being scrapped.
But this is one of just five “everyday fixes” announced this morning. Here is what the Treasury says about them.

double quotation mark• Making higher tax-free mileage rates permanent and increasing support for nurses, care workers, self employed builders and others who drive for work. The chancellor is locking in the 55p per mile rate for the first 10,000 business miles and increasing the rate above 10,000 miles from 25p to 35p per mile, supporting around 3 million employees and self-employed people who use their own vehicle for work. • Extending parental pay to more than 150,000 additional parents per year, including self-employed dads and partners who have previously missed out, giving eligible parents two weeks of support currently worth up to £194 a week so they can spend more time with their child. • Ending the Carer’s Allowance cliff edge, so unpaid carers no longer lose their entire allowance simply for earning a penny over the Weekly Earnings Limit, equivalent to 16 hours of the National Living Wage. Instead, only £1 of support will taper away for every additional £1 earned. • Removing import tariffs on more than 100 products, helping lower import costs on family favourites including baked beans, chocolate and gherkins, while also supporting farmers facing higher fertiliser bills and households that rely on kerosene heating oil. Together with tariff suspensions already introduced, households could save up to £21 on their food shop each year. • Rolling out hundreds more Post Office drop boxes, bringing the total to 1,000, making it easier and more convenient for people to send and return parcels without having to queue at a Post Office counter, helping take some of the hassle out of everyday errands in the run-up to Christmas. This comes alongside upgrades to 600 Post Office branches by the end of the financial year, improving services for customers across the country.
There is more detail in the Treasury news release here.
It is always easy to mock, and the Conservatives could not resist. Here is their response, from Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor.

double quotation markRampant borrowing, soaring taxes and an utter inability to cut spending mean inflation has already wiped out the benefits of Burnham’s ‘everyday fixes’. Shoppers face rising costs at the till and families are struggling to make ends meet, but Burnham’s plan is cheaper gherkins. This is an insult to families hammered by Labour’s tax rises.

The mention of gherkins in the Treasury press release did come as a surprise, given that they are not a key feature of the national diet, but maybe someone in Whitehall read the reports earlier this year about their importance for Pret a Manger sandwiches.
The problem with the Tory response is that, even though “everyday fixes” might not make a big difference, people tend to welcome them anyway. This is from Novara Media’s Aaron Bastani.

double quotation markPart of the genius with this stuff is the negative polarisation, when people start attacking perfectly sensible and helpful – albeit small – changes. Actually I want longer Post Office queues please!
Here is the agenda for the day.
10.30am: Sarah Sackman, the courts minister, gives evidence to the Lords justice committee on support for jurors.
Morning: Andy Burnham hosts a meeting with Muslim leaders in No 10.
11.30am: Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, takes questions in the Commons.
Noon: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
After 12.30pm: Dan Jarvis, the security minister, is expected to give a statement to MPs about the government’s ‘Be Ready’ resilience advice about stockpiling essentials.
